summary: Friedrich Creuzer (1771–1858) worked in religious studies, philosophy, and history and archaeology. He studied at Tübingen (~1789–1791) and Jena (~1791–1794), and held posts at Marburg (~1802–1804), Heidelberg (~1804–1845), and Leiden (1809).

Friedrich Delitzsch (1850–1922) was a scholar of linguistics and history and archaeology. He studied at Leipzig and Berlin under Brockhaus, Curtius, Windisch, Fleischer, and Dillmann. He held posts at Breslau (~1893–1899) and Berlin (~1899–1920).
Friedrich Ernst August Krause (1879–1942) worked in sinology. He studied at the Seminar für Orientalische Sprachen (~1902–1905) and held a post at Heidelberg University (~1921–1942).

Friedrich Gottlieb Welcker (1784–1868) worked in history, archaeology, and linguistics. He studied at the University of Giessen (~1801–1803) and held posts at Giessen (~1808–1816), Göttingen (~1816–1819), and Bonn (~1819–1861).

Friedrich Haag (1846–1914) studied at Zurich under Heinrich Schweizer-Sidler, as well as at Göttingen and Berlin. He taught at Zurich, Tallinn, Schaffhausen, and Burgdorf, and was professor of classical philology at Bern from 1887 to 1906.

Friedrich Heiler (1892–1967) worked in religious studies. He studied at the University of Munich (~1912–1917), where he taught in 1918, before holding posts at the University of Marburg (1920) and the Religionskundliche Sammlung (~1927–1962).

Friedrich Hirth (1845–1927) worked in sinology and history and archaeology. He studied at Leipzig, Berlin, and Greifswald, and served with the Chinese Maritime Customs Service (1870–1897) before becoming Dean Lung Professor of Chinese at Columbia University (1902).
Friedrich Kurschat (1806–1884) was a linguist. He studied at the University of Königsberg from ~1836 to 1840 and subsequently held a post there from ~1840 to 1883.
Friedrich Leo (1851–1914) worked in linguistics. He studied at Göttingen and Bonn, the latter under Hermann Usener. He held posts at Bonn, Kiel, Rostock, Strasbourg, and Göttingen (1889–1914).

Friedrich Majer (1772–1818) worked in Indology and history and archaeology. He studied at the University of Jena (~1789–1792) and under Johann Gottfried von Herder (~1797–1803), later serving as a Privatdozent at Jena.

Friedrich Max Müller (1823–1900) worked in Indology, religious studies, and linguistics. He studied at Leipzig, Berlin, and Paris under Brockhaus, Bopp, Schelling, and Burnouf, and under Wilson. He held posts at Oxford from 1850, including professor from 1868 to 1900.

Friedrich Müller (1834–1898) worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied at Vienna, Göttingen, and Tübingen, learning under Anton Boller. He worked at the Vienna University Library and Austrian National Library, and was professor at Vienna from 1869.

Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) worked in philosophy and linguistics. He studied at the universities of Bonn and Leipzig, studying under Friedrich Wilhelm Ritschl, and held a faculty post at the University of Basel from 1869 to 1878.

Friedrich Otto Schrader (1876–1961) worked in Indology and philosophy. He earned his doctorate at the University of Strasbourg (~1899–1902), directed the Adyar Library and Research Centre (1905–1916), and became a professor at Kiel University in 1921.
Friedrich Ottomar Eduard Wilhelm (1882–1939) held university posts at the University of Munich (~1910–1923) and the University of Freiburg (~1923–1939).
Friedrich Rosen (1805–1837) completed doctoral studies under Franz Bopp (~1824–1826) and served as Professor of Sanskrit at the University of London from ~1828 to 1837.

Friedrich Rückert (1788–1866) worked in Indology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He studied at Würzburg, Heidelberg, and under Bopp and von Hammer-Purgstall. He held posts at Jena (1811), Erlangen-Nuremberg (1826), and Berlin (1841–1849).

Friedrich Schlegel (1772–1829) worked in Indology, linguistics, and philosophy. He studied at Göttingen and Leipzig, and under Heyne, Hamilton, and Chézy. He held posts at Jena (1800), Cologne (1804), and TU Dresden (1828).

Friedrich Schleiermacher (1768–1834) was a philosopher and religious studies scholar. He studied at Halle-Wittenberg (~1787–1789), where he later held a post (~1804–1807), followed by a chair at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1810–1834).

Friedrich Schrader (1865–1922) was a scholar in Indology and history and archaeology. He completed his doctoral studies at Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (~1885–1889) under the supervision of Richard Pischel.
